definition: The plasma membrane is a bilayer of phospholipids with their hydrophobic fatty acid tails facing each other, studded with proteins (some spanning the membrane, some transporting materials) and with carbohydrates attached on the outward-facing surface that identify the cell.
intro: What the membrane every cell has is actually made of.

constraints.text: The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with the hydrophobic tails inside, facing each other.
Proteins are embedded in or span the membrane; some transport materials in or out.
Carbohydrates attach to proteins and lipids on the outward-facing surface and identify the cell to other cells.

misconceptions.label: tails face the water
misconceptions.description: The hydrophilic heads point into the middle of the bilayer and the tails face the water.

misconceptions.label: the membrane is rigid
misconceptions.description: The membrane is a fixed, static wall whose parts do not move.

title: Membrane fluidity
definition: Membrane fluidity depends on temperature, on how the fatty acid tails are configured (double bonds kink them and keep them from packing), on cholesterol embedded in the membrane, and on proteins not being fixed in place.
intro: Why a membrane stays fluid enough to work at different temperatures.

constraints.text: Unsaturated (kinked) fatty acid tails pack less tightly and keep the membrane more fluid.
Cholesterol embedded in the membrane helps maintain its fluidity across temperatures.
Fluidity rises with temperature and falls in the cold.

misconceptions.label: saturated tails increase fluidity
misconceptions.description: More saturated fatty acids make a membrane more fluid.

misconceptions.label: cholesterol only stiffens
misconceptions.description: Cholesterol can only ever make a membrane less fluid.

title: Diffusion
definition: Substances diffuse from areas of high concentration to areas of lower concentration until evenly distributed, each down its own gradient independent of the others. Diffusion is passive transport: the cell spends none of its energy. Its rate depends on the concentration gradient, particle size and temperature.
intro: Movement downhill, for free.

constraints.text: Diffusion moves a substance from high to low concentration, down its gradient, until it is evenly distributed.
Diffusion is passive transport: it needs no energy from the cell.
Its rate depends on the concentration gradient, particle size and temperature.

misconceptions.label: diffusion uses ATP
misconceptions.description: Diffusion needs ATP to push molecules through the membrane.

misconceptions.label: all solutes share one gradient
misconceptions.description: In a mixture, every solute diffuses down one shared concentration gradient.

title: Facilitated diffusion
definition: In facilitated diffusion (facilitated transport), materials diffuse across the plasma membrane with the help of integral membrane proteins, channels or carriers, moving down their concentration gradient; substances whose passage the membrane hinders cross this way.
intro: Still downhill, but through a protein door.

constraints.text: Facilitated diffusion uses integral membrane proteins that act as channels or carriers.
It moves material down its concentration gradient, from high to low concentration.

misconceptions.label: a carrier means active transport
misconceptions.description: Any transport that uses a carrier protein is active transport.

misconceptions.label: carriers move substances uphill
misconceptions.description: Facilitated diffusion moves substances against their gradient.

title: Osmosis
definition: Osmosis is the transport of water through a semipermeable membrane down the concentration gradient of water, a gradient set up by solute that cannot cross the membrane; so water moves toward the side with the higher solute concentration.
intro: Water follows solute.

constraints.text: In osmosis water moves from lower to higher solute concentration (from higher to lower water concentration).
The gradient that drives osmosis comes from solute that cannot pass through the membrane.

misconceptions.label: solute moves in osmosis
misconceptions.description: In osmosis the solute crosses the membrane toward the side with less solute.

misconceptions.label: water moves toward less solute
misconceptions.description: Water moves toward the side with the lower solute concentration.

title: Tonicity
definition: Tonicity describes how the concentration of solutes outside a cell that cannot cross its membrane changes the cell's volume by affecting osmosis: in a hypotonic solution (lower osmolarity outside) water enters and the cell swells and may burst; in a hypertonic one water leaves; in an isotonic one there is no net movement.
intro: Will the cell swell, shrink, or stay the same?

constraints.text: In a hypotonic solution water enters the cell, which swells and may burst.
In a hypertonic solution water leaves the cell.
In an isotonic solution there is no net movement of water.

misconceptions.label: hypotonic shrinks cells
misconceptions.description: A cell placed in a hypotonic solution loses water and shrinks.

misconceptions.label: isotonic means water stops
misconceptions.description: In an isotonic solution water molecules stop crossing the membrane.

title: Active transport
definition: Active transport moves substances up their electrochemical gradient using energy, through membrane pumps. Primary active transport couples directly to ATP (the sodium-potassium pump); in co-transport (secondary active transport) the gradient a primary pump made drives another substance up its gradient.
intro: Uphill movement, paid for in ATP.

constraints.text: Active transport moves a substance against its (electro)chemical gradient and requires energy.
Primary active transport uses ATP directly, e.g. the Na+/K+ pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in).
Secondary active transport (co-transport) uses a gradient made by a primary pump, so it depends on ATP indirectly.

misconceptions.label: secondary uses ATP directly
misconceptions.description: Secondary active transport hydrolyzes ATP directly at the transporter.

misconceptions.label: active transport is downhill
misconceptions.description: Active transport moves substances down their gradient, only faster.

title: Endocytosis and exocytosis
definition: Bulk transport moves large particles into or out of the cell in membrane-bound vesicles and requires energy. In endocytosis the membrane invaginates and pinches off around material: phagocytosis engulfs large particles, pinocytosis takes in extracellular fluid, receptor-mediated endocytosis takes in one targeted substance bound to receptors. In exocytosis a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside.
intro: How a cell moves things too big for any channel or pump.

constraints.text: Phagocytosis engulfs large particles ('cell eating'); pinocytosis takes in extracellular fluid ('cell drinking').
In exocytosis a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, becomes part of it, and releases its contents outside.
Taking in and releasing large particles requires energy.
Receptor-mediated endocytosis brings in only a specifically targeted substance bound to receptors.

misconceptions.label: bulk transport is passive
misconceptions.description: Endocytosis and exocytosis need no energy from the cell.

misconceptions.label: exocytosis brings things in
misconceptions.description: Exocytosis is how a cell takes material in.

title: Anabolism and catabolism
definition: A cell's metabolism is all of its chemical reactions. Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler ones and releases energy; anabolism builds complex molecules from simpler ones and requires energy. Glucose breakdown is catabolic; glucose synthesis is anabolic.
intro: Two directions of chemistry in every cell.

constraints.text: Catabolism breaks complex molecules down and releases energy.
Anabolism builds complex molecules from simpler ones and requires energy.

misconceptions.label: anabolism releases energy
misconceptions.description: Anabolic reactions break molecules down and release energy.

misconceptions.label: cells do only one
misconceptions.description: A cell is either anabolic or catabolic, not both.

title: Free energy: exergonic and endergonic
definition: Free energy (G) is the energy available to do work. A reaction with negative ΔG releases energy, is exergonic and spontaneous (products have less energy than reactants); one with positive ΔG consumes energy, is endergonic and nonspontaneous.
intro: The sign of ΔG says which way a reaction can go on its own.

constraints.text: Negative ΔG = exergonic, releases energy, spontaneous; positive ΔG = endergonic, requires energy, nonspontaneous.
Exergonic products have less free energy than reactants; endergonic products have more.
Spontaneous does not mean fast: ΔG says nothing about the rate.

misconceptions.label: spontaneous means fast
misconceptions.description: A spontaneous (−ΔG) reaction happens quickly.

misconceptions.label: positive ΔG releases energy
misconceptions.description: A reaction with a positive ΔG releases energy.

title: Activation energy
definition: All reactions, even spontaneous ones, need an initial input of energy, the activation energy, to reach the transition state at which they proceed. Activation energy is lower if the reaction is catalyzed.
intro: The hill every reaction must climb first.

constraints.text: Every reaction, including spontaneous (−ΔG) ones, needs activation energy to reach the transition state.
A catalyst (enzyme) lowers the activation energy but does not change the free energy (ΔG) of the reaction.

misconceptions.label: exergonic reactions need no activation energy
misconceptions.description: Exergonic reactions start by themselves with no energy input.

misconceptions.label: enzymes change ΔG
misconceptions.description: An enzyme makes a reaction release more energy by changing its ΔG.

title: The first law of thermodynamics
definition: The first law of thermodynamics: the total amount of energy in the universe is constant, so energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed.
intro: Cells never make energy; they move it around.

constraints.text: The total energy of the universe is constant; energy is transferred or transformed, never created or destroyed.
A cell does not make energy: it transforms energy it takes in (food or light) into other forms, including heat.

misconceptions.label: cells create energy
misconceptions.description: Cells create new energy from food.

misconceptions.label: used energy is destroyed
misconceptions.description: Energy a cell uses up is destroyed.

title: The second law of thermodynamics
definition: The second law of thermodynamics: every energy transfer loses some energy in an unusable form such as heat, so no transfer is completely efficient and systems tend toward disorder (higher entropy). Making a system more ordered, lower in entropy, takes energy.
intro: Why every transfer leaks heat, and why order costs energy.

constraints.text: Every energy transfer loses some energy as unusable heat and tends toward disorder (entropy rises).
Entropy measures disorder; making a system more ordered (lower entropy) takes energy.

misconceptions.label: transfers can be 100% efficient
misconceptions.description: Some energy transfers in cells lose no energy at all.

misconceptions.label: living things break the second law
misconceptions.description: A cell's high order shows that living things violate the second law.

title: ATP
definition: ATP, the primary energy-supplying molecule of living cells, is a nucleotide with a five-carbon sugar and three phosphate groups; the bonds between its phosphates have high energy, and the energy released by hydrolyzing ATP into ADP + Pi is used to do cellular work.
intro: The cell's energy currency.

constraints.text: ATP is a nucleotide with a five-carbon sugar and three phosphate groups.
Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP + Pi releases energy that cells use for work.

misconceptions.label: breaking the bond stores energy
misconceptions.description: Breaking the phosphate bond of ATP absorbs energy that the cell stores.

misconceptions.label: ATP is long-term storage
misconceptions.description: ATP is the cell's long-term energy store, like fat.

title: Energy coupling
definition: Energy coupling: cells drive endergonic reactions by coupling them to the exergonic hydrolysis of ATP; ATP donates its phosphate group to another molecule (phosphorylation), which puts that molecule in a higher-energy, less stable state that lets its endergonic reaction go.
intro: How the energy of ATP gets spent on an uphill reaction.

constraints.text: The exergonic reaction of ATP hydrolysis is coupled with endergonic reactions.
Coupling works by phosphorylation: ATP donates its phosphate to another molecule, raising its energy.

misconceptions.label: ATP heats the reaction
misconceptions.description: ATP drives a reaction by releasing heat that the reactants absorb.

misconceptions.label: endergonic reactions just need time
misconceptions.description: An endergonic reaction will go on its own if given enough time.

title: Enzymes
definition: Enzymes are chemical catalysts, usually proteins, that speed up reactions by lowering their activation energy without changing the reaction's free energy. The substrate binds the active site, made of particular R groups, with an induced fit; each enzyme is matched to specific substrates and is left unchanged by the reaction it catalyzes.
intro: Protein catalysts: specific, reusable, and shape-dependent.

constraints.text: Enzymes speed reactions by lowering activation energy; they do not change the free energy (ΔG).
The substrate binds the active site, with an induced fit (the enzyme changes shape slightly on binding).
Enzymes remain unchanged by the reactions they catalyze and are matched to specific substrates.

misconceptions.label: enzymes are used up
misconceptions.description: An enzyme is used up in the reaction it catalyzes.

misconceptions.label: the active site is rigid
misconceptions.description: The active site is rigid; the substrate fits it like a key with no change in shape.

misconceptions.label: enzymes change ΔG
misconceptions.description: An enzyme speeds a reaction by making it release more energy.

title: Enzyme inhibition
definition: Inhibitors regulate enzymes in two ways. A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and competes with the substrate for it; a noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere, at an allosteric site. Competitive inhibitors lower the initial rate but not the maximal rate; noncompetitive inhibitors lower the maximal rate.
intro: Two ways to slow an enzyme down.

constraints.text: A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and competes with the substrate.
A noncompetitive inhibitor binds an allosteric site, away from the active site, and lowers the maximal rate.
Competitive inhibitors do not change the maximal rate (enough substrate outcompetes them); noncompetitive inhibitors lower it.

misconceptions.label: competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere
misconceptions.description: A competitive inhibitor binds an allosteric site away from the active site.

misconceptions.label: more substrate beats any inhibitor
misconceptions.description: Adding more substrate overcomes a noncompetitive inhibitor.

title: Feedback inhibition
definition: Feedback inhibition is the most common way cells regulate the enzymes of a metabolic pathway: the end product of the pathway inhibits (usually allosterically) an upstream enzyme, usually the first committed enzyme, so the product shuts down its own further production.
intro: A pathway that switches itself off when it has made enough.

constraints.text: In feedback inhibition the end product of a pathway inhibits an upstream enzyme of that pathway.
The enzyme inhibited is usually the first committed enzyme, often allosterically.

misconceptions.label: the product speeds its own pathway
misconceptions.description: In feedback inhibition the product activates the first enzyme to make more of itself.

misconceptions.label: the last enzyme is inhibited
misconceptions.description: The end product inhibits only the final enzyme of its pathway.

title: Glycolysis
definition: Glycolysis, in the cytoplasm and without using oxygen, splits one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvate. Two ATP are invested and four made by substrate-level phosphorylation, a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.
intro: The first, oldest and most universal step of breaking down glucose.

constraints.text: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and does not use oxygen.
One glucose (6C) becomes two pyruvate (3C).
2 ATP invested, 4 ATP made: net 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.

misconceptions.label: glycolysis is in the mitochondria
misconceptions.description: Glycolysis takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.

misconceptions.label: glycolysis needs oxygen
misconceptions.description: Glycolysis can only run when oxygen is present.

title: Pyruvate oxidation
definition: With oxygen present, each pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is converted to an acetyl group carried by coenzyme A (acetyl CoA); one CO2 is removed and NAD+ is reduced to NADH.
intro: The bridge from glycolysis into the mitochondrion.

constraints.text: Pyruvate is converted into acetyl CoA (an acetyl group on coenzyme A).
One CO2 is released and one NADH made per pyruvate.
It takes place in the mitochondrial matrix, after pyruvate enters the mitochondrion.

misconceptions.label: it makes ATP directly
misconceptions.description: Converting pyruvate to acetyl CoA produces ATP directly.

misconceptions.label: oxygen is removed
misconceptions.description: Oxygen is the molecule removed from pyruvate.

title: The citric acid cycle
definition: In the mitochondrial matrix the citric acid (Krebs) cycle runs redox and decarboxylation reactions that remove carbon dioxide and high-energy electrons. Each turn produces two CO2, three NADH, one FADH2 and one ATP or GTP by substrate-level phosphorylation; the NADH and FADH2 carry the electrons on to make ATP in a later pathway.
intro: Where the last carbons of glucose leave as CO2.

constraints.text: The cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix.
Per turn: 2 CO2, 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 ATP/GTP (substrate-level phosphorylation).
The electrons stored in NADH and FADH2 are used to make ATP in a later pathway.

misconceptions.label: the cycle makes most of the ATP
misconceptions.description: The citric acid cycle makes most of the ATP of respiration directly.

misconceptions.label: the cycle is in the cytoplasm
misconceptions.description: The citric acid cycle takes place in the cytoplasm.

misconceptions.label: the cycle uses O2 directly
misconceptions.description: Oxygen is consumed in the citric acid cycle itself.

title: The electron transport chain
definition: Protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane pass electrons from NADH and FADH2 down a series of redox reactions; the energy released pumps H+ into the intermembrane space. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and is reduced to water.
intro: Why we breathe oxygen.

constraints.text: The chain is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane (the cristae).
Electrons from NADH/FADH2 lose energy step by step; that energy pumps H+ across the membrane.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor; it is reduced to water.

misconceptions.label: oxygen becomes CO2
misconceptions.description: The oxygen we breathe becomes the carbon dioxide we breathe out.

misconceptions.label: the chain itself makes ATP
misconceptions.description: The electron carriers of the chain phosphorylate ADP directly.

title: Chemiosmosis
definition: Chemiosmosis is making ATP with a proton gradient across a membrane: protons driven down their gradient through the membrane protein ATP synthase power it to add a phosphate to ADP. In mitochondria this is called oxidative phosphorylation, and it makes about 90 percent of the ATP of aerobic glucose catabolism.
intro: The turbine that turns a proton gradient into ATP.

constraints.text: H+ flows down its gradient through ATP synthase.
ATP synthase uses the energy of that flow to make ATP from ADP and Pi.
Chemiosmosis in mitochondria (oxidative phosphorylation) makes about 90% of the ATP from aerobic glucose catabolism.

misconceptions.label: electrons pass through ATP synthase
misconceptions.description: Electrons, not protons, flow through ATP synthase.

misconceptions.label: a leaky membrane helps
misconceptions.description: If H+ could leak across the membrane freely, more ATP would be made.

title: Fermentation
definition: Without oxygen, cells regenerate NAD+ by fermentation so glycolysis can continue: in lactic acid fermentation (animals, some bacteria) pyruvate is reduced to lactate; in alcohol fermentation (yeast) pyruvate becomes ethanol. Regenerating NAD+ makes no ATP, so a cell that cannot break pyruvate down further gets only glycolysis's two ATP per glucose.
intro: Keeping glycolysis going when oxygen runs out.

constraints.text: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue without oxygen.
Lactic acid fermentation (animals) makes lactate; alcohol fermentation (yeast) makes ethanol.
Fermentation makes no extra ATP: the yield is glycolysis's 2 ATP per glucose.

misconceptions.label: fermentation makes lots of ATP
misconceptions.description: Fermentation itself produces most of the ATP when oxygen is absent.

misconceptions.label: muscle makes ethanol
misconceptions.description: Human muscle cells make ethanol when they run short of oxygen.

title: Photosynthesis overview
definition: Photoautotrophs, which have chlorophyll, use energy from sunlight to assemble carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. In plants and algae this happens in chloroplasts: the light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid membrane, the Calvin cycle in the stroma. Plants still respire too: they contain both chloroplasts and mitochondria.
intro: The reverse of respiration, powered by sunlight.

constraints.text: Photosynthesis uses CO2 and water (and light) to make carbohydrate, releasing O2.
In eukaryotes it occurs in chloroplasts: light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid membrane, Calvin cycle in the stroma.
Plants need both photosynthesis and cellular respiration, so they contain both chloroplasts and mitochondria.

misconceptions.label: plants do not respire
misconceptions.description: Plants photosynthesize instead of doing cellular respiration.

misconceptions.label: the O2 comes from CO2
misconceptions.description: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from carbon dioxide.

title: The light-dependent reactions
definition: The light-dependent reactions, in the thylakoid membrane, use light to make ATP and NADPH. Light absorbed in photosystem II splits water, releasing oxygen, and the water's electrons replace those boosted from the reaction center; the electron transport chain pumps hydrogen ions into the thylakoid interior, they flow back through ATP synthase to make ATP, and photosystem I absorbs a second photon to make NADPH.
intro: Turning light into ATP and NADPH.

constraints.text: The light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membrane.
Water is split in photosystem II to replace its electrons; this releases O2.
They make ATP (by chemiosmosis through ATP synthase) and NADPH, which power the Calvin cycle.

misconceptions.label: light reactions make sugar
misconceptions.description: The light-dependent reactions produce glucose directly.

misconceptions.label: light reactions are in the stroma
misconceptions.description: The light-dependent reactions take place in the stroma.

title: The Calvin cycle
definition: The Calvin cycle (the light-independent reactions), in the stroma, uses the energy carriers made by the light-dependent reactions to take in CO2: the enzyme RuBisCO catalyzes the reaction of CO2 with RuBP; after three turns one three-carbon G3P leaves to become part of a carbohydrate, and the remaining G3P regenerates RuBP.
intro: Where carbon from the air becomes sugar.

constraints.text: The Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions) occurs in the stroma.
RuBisCO catalyzes the reaction of CO2 with RuBP.
It runs on energy carriers from the light reactions; its product is G3P, and the rest of the G3P regenerates RuBP.

misconceptions.label: it runs only in the dark
misconceptions.description: The Calvin cycle happens only at night.

misconceptions.label: it fixes oxygen
misconceptions.description: The Calvin cycle takes in O2 from the air to build sugar.

title: Types of cell signaling
definition: Signaling cells release ligands that bind receptors on target cells. Paracrine signals act over short distances on nearby cells; endocrine signals (hormones) travel long distances in the blood; autocrine signals act on the cell that released them (or its own kind); gap junctions pass signals directly between neighbouring cells.
intro: Four ways cells talk, sorted by distance.

constraints.text: Paracrine signaling acts over short distances on nearby cells.
Endocrine signals are hormones carried long distances by the bloodstream (slower).
Autocrine signals act on the sending cell itself; direct signaling passes small molecules through gap junctions.

misconceptions.label: endocrine signals are fastest
misconceptions.description: Endocrine signals act faster than paracrine signals because the blood moves quickly.

misconceptions.label: autocrine means distant
misconceptions.description: Autocrine signals travel to distant organs.

title: Internal and cell-surface receptors
definition: Small hydrophobic ligands such as steroids cross the plasma membrane and bind internal receptors that act on DNA directly. Hydrophilic ligands cannot cross, so they bind cell-surface receptors: ion channel-linked, G-protein-linked, or enzyme-linked (e.g. receptor tyrosine kinases).
intro: Where a signal is received depends on whether it can cross the membrane.

constraints.text: Hydrophobic ligands (steroids, gases like NO) cross the membrane and bind internal receptors that regulate gene expression.
Hydrophilic ligands cannot cross the bilayer and bind cell-surface receptors.
Cell-surface receptors are ion channel-linked, G-protein-linked or enzyme-linked.

misconceptions.label: steroids bind surface receptors
misconceptions.description: Steroid hormones bind G-protein-linked receptors on the cell surface.

misconceptions.label: every ligand enters the cell
misconceptions.description: All signaling molecules must enter the cell to act.

title: Signal transduction cascades
definition: Ligand binding to a receptor starts signal transduction: a chain of events, the signaling pathway or cascade, carries the signal through the cell. Kinases phosphorylate proteins on serine, threonine and tyrosine, changing their shape to activate or inactivate them; one activated receptor-linked enzyme can activate many copies of the next component, amplifying the signal. Phosphatases and the degradation of signaling molecules terminate it.
intro: How one molecule outside changes what happens inside.

constraints.text: Kinases phosphorylate proteins (serine, threonine, tyrosine residues) to activate or inactivate them along a cascade.
Each activated enzyme can activate many copies of the next component, which amplifies the signal.
Phosphatases remove phosphates and signaling molecules are degraded, which terminates the signal.

misconceptions.label: one ligand affects one protein
misconceptions.description: Each ligand molecule can change only one protein inside the cell.

misconceptions.label: a cascade cannot be switched off
misconceptions.description: Once a cascade starts, nothing in the cell can stop it.

title: Second messengers
definition: Second messengers are small, non-protein molecules, such as Ca2+, cyclic AMP (cAMP), diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol triphosphate (IP3), that carry a signal inside the cell after a ligand, the first messenger, has bound its receptor.
intro: The small molecules that carry a signal once it is inside.

constraints.text: Second messengers are small non-protein molecules that transmit the signal within the cell.
Examples are Ca2+, cAMP, DAG and IP3.

misconceptions.label: the first messenger enters
misconceptions.description: In a G-protein pathway the hormone itself enters the cell and becomes the second messenger.

misconceptions.label: second messengers are proteins
misconceptions.description: Second messengers are large signaling proteins such as kinases.

title: Diploid and haploid
definition: Human somatic cells have 46 chromosomes, 22 pairs of autosomes and a pair of sex chromosomes: two sets, the diploid (2n) state. Human gametes have 23 chromosomes, one complete set: the haploid (n) state.
intro: Counting chromosome sets: the vocabulary every division question assumes.

constraints.text: Diploid (2n) somatic cells have two sets of chromosomes: 46 in humans (22 pairs of autosomes + 2 sex chromosomes).
Haploid (n) gametes have one complete set: 23 chromosomes in humans.

misconceptions.label: gametes have 46
misconceptions.description: Human egg and sperm cells each carry 46 chromosomes.

misconceptions.label: haploid cells have pairs
misconceptions.description: A haploid cell has 23 pairs of chromosomes.

title: The cell cycle
definition: The eukaryotic cell cycle is a long preparatory interphase, divided into Gap 1 (G1), DNA synthesis (S) and Gap 2 (G2), followed by the mitotic phase: mitosis (karyokinesis) and then cytokinesis. DNA is replicated in the S phase.
intro: Most of a cell's life is spent getting ready to divide.

constraints.text: Interphase = G1, S (DNA synthesis) and G2, before the mitotic phase.
DNA is replicated in the S phase, forming sister chromatids.
The mitotic phase is mitosis (karyokinesis) followed by cytokinesis.

misconceptions.label: interphase is a resting phase
misconceptions.description: Interphase is a resting phase in which the cell does nothing.

misconceptions.label: DNA is copied during mitosis
misconceptions.description: Chromosomes are duplicated during prophase of mitosis.

title: Homologs vs sister chromatids
definition: Homologous chromosomes are a matched pair with the same genes in the same locations, one from each parent. Sister chromatids are the two identical DNA molecules made when one chromosome is replicated in S phase, firmly attached at the centromere.
intro: Two kinds of chromosome 'pair' that every division question tells apart.

constraints.text: Homologous chromosomes carry the same genes in the same locations; one comes from each parent.
Sister chromatids are the two identical copies made by replicating one chromosome, joined at the centromere.

misconceptions.label: homologs are identical
misconceptions.description: Homologous chromosomes are genetically identical copies.

misconceptions.label: sister chromatids come from each parent
misconceptions.description: One sister chromatid comes from the mother and one from the father.

title: Stages of mitosis
definition: Mitosis (karyokinesis) divides the nucleus in five stages: prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. Sister chromatids line up at the metaphase plate in metaphase and separate at the centromere in anaphase, so the duplicated chromosomes are aligned, separated and moved into two identical daughter cells.
intro: Dividing the copied chromosomes evenly between two nuclei.

constraints.text: Prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.
Sister chromatids line up at the metaphase plate in metaphase and separate in anaphase.
Mitosis gives two daughter cells genetically identical to the parent.

misconceptions.label: mitosis halves the chromosomes
misconceptions.description: Each daughter cell from mitosis has half the parent's chromosomes.

misconceptions.label: homologs separate in anaphase
misconceptions.description: In mitotic anaphase homologous chromosomes are pulled apart.

title: Cytokinesis
definition: Cytokinesis, the final stage of the mitotic phase, separates the cytoplasm into two daughter cells: in animal cells an actin ring contracts and forms a cleavage furrow; in plant cells a cell plate forms and grows into a new cell wall.
intro: Splitting one cell into two after the nucleus has divided.

constraints.text: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm after mitosis, the last stage of the mitotic phase.
Animal cells divide by a contracting actin ring that forms a cleavage furrow.
Plant cells divide by a cell plate that grows into a new cell wall.

misconceptions.label: plant cells pinch in two
misconceptions.description: Plant cells divide by a cleavage furrow, like animal cells.

misconceptions.label: cytokinesis is part of mitosis
misconceptions.description: Cytokinesis is the stage of mitosis that separates the sister chromatids.

title: Cell cycle checkpoints
definition: Internal controls called checkpoints, near the end of G1, at the G2/M transition and during metaphase, monitor the cell cycle. Positive regulators, cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdks), let it advance; negative regulators such as Rb and p53 can halt it until requirements are met. p53 stops the cycle when DNA is damaged and can trigger apoptosis if it cannot be repaired.
intro: The brakes and accelerator of division.

constraints.text: Three main checkpoints: near the end of G1, at G2/M, and during metaphase.
Cyclins and Cdks are positive regulators; Rb and p53 are negative regulators that can halt the cycle.
p53 halts the cycle when DNA is damaged and can trigger apoptosis if it cannot be repaired.

misconceptions.label: p53 drives division
misconceptions.description: p53 is a positive regulator that pushes the cell into S phase.

misconceptions.label: the cycle runs unchecked
misconceptions.description: Once started, the cell cycle runs to completion with no internal checks.

title: Cancer
definition: Cancer is unchecked cell division caused by a breakdown of cell cycle control, beginning with a change in the DNA of a gene for a regulatory molecule. Proto-oncogenes, the genes for positive regulators, can mutate into oncogenes that cause a cell to become cancerous; tumor suppressor genes code for negative regulators that can prevent uncontrolled division, so losing them removes a brake.
intro: What happens when the brakes and accelerator of division fail.

constraints.text: Cancer is unchecked division caused by mutations in genes for cell cycle regulators.
Proto-oncogenes code for positive regulators; mutated, they become oncogenes.
Tumor suppressor genes code for negative regulators that can prevent uncontrolled division.

misconceptions.label: one mutation causes cancer
misconceptions.description: A single mutation in any gene is enough to cause cancer.

misconceptions.label: proto-oncogenes are abnormal
misconceptions.description: Proto-oncogenes are abnormal genes that only cancer cells carry.

title: Binary fission
definition: Prokaryotes divide by binary fission. Bacteria have one circular chromosome and no nucleus, so mitosis is not needed: replication starts at the origin, and the two origins move apart toward opposite ends of the cell. A ring of the protein FtsZ directs cytokinesis, and a septum grows in that becomes the daughter cells' walls.
intro: How a cell with no nucleus divides.

constraints.text: Binary fission needs no mitosis: bacteria have no nucleus and one circular chromosome.
An FtsZ protein ring directs cytokinesis; a septum forms the new cell walls.
Replication starts at the origin, and the copies' origins move to opposite ends of the cell.

misconceptions.label: bacteria use a mitotic spindle
misconceptions.description: A mitotic spindle pulls the bacterial chromosome copies apart.

misconceptions.label: fission is meiosis
misconceptions.description: Binary fission halves the chromosome number like meiosis.

title: DNA double helix structure
definition: DNA is a double helix of two complementary, antiparallel strands whose backbone is deoxyribose sugars and phosphates, with the nitrogenous bases stacked inside. A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, A with T and G with C; the pairs are held by hydrogen bonds, two between A and T and three between G and C.
intro: The structure that makes copying possible.

constraints.text: The two strands are complementary and antiparallel (one 5'→3', the other 3'→5').
A pairs with T and G pairs with C; a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine.
A–T pairs form two hydrogen bonds; G–C pairs form three.
Because A pairs only with T and G only with C, %A = %T and %G = %C.

misconceptions.label: the strands run the same way
misconceptions.description: Both DNA strands run in the same 5'→3' direction.

misconceptions.label: A pairs with G
misconceptions.description: Purines pair with purines: A pairs with G.

title: DNA replication
definition: Replication is semiconservative: each new double helix keeps one parental strand. Helicase opens the helix at the origin, primase lays an RNA primer, and DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only 5'→3', continuously on the leading strand and in Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand; ligase seals the fragments.
intro: Copying the genome before every division.

constraints.text: Replication is semiconservative: each daughter helix has one old and one new strand.
Helicase unwinds; primase makes an RNA primer; DNA polymerase extends 5'→3'; ligase joins fragments.
The leading strand is made continuously; the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments.

misconceptions.label: the old helix stays whole
misconceptions.description: Replication keeps the original double helix intact and builds a wholly new one.

misconceptions.label: polymerase works 3'→5'
misconceptions.description: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides in the 3'→5' direction.

title: Meiosis
definition: Meiosis follows one round of DNA replication with two divisions, giving four haploid cells that are genetically unique. Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes (the reduction division); meiosis II separates sister chromatids, like mitosis. Variation comes from crossing over in prophase I and the random alignment of tetrads at metaphase I.
intro: The division that makes gametes, and the variation that comes with it.

constraints.text: One replication and two divisions give four haploid, genetically different cells.
Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes (reduces ploidy); meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
Variation comes from crossing over (prophase I) and independent assortment of tetrads at metaphase I.

misconceptions.label: meiosis II halves the number
misconceptions.description: The chromosome number is halved in meiosis II, when sister chromatids separate.

misconceptions.label: meiosis gives identical cells
misconceptions.description: The four cells from meiosis are genetically identical.

title: The central dogma
definition: The central dogma describes the flow of genetic information in the cell from genes to mRNA to proteins: genes are used to make mRNA by transcription, and mRNA is used to make proteins by translation.
intro: DNA to RNA to protein, the order everything else follows.

constraints.text: Genetic information flows from DNA (genes) to mRNA to protein.
DNA → mRNA is transcription; mRNA → protein is translation.

misconceptions.label: proteins are templates for DNA
misconceptions.description: A cell copies its proteins back into DNA to store them.

misconceptions.label: translation makes RNA
misconceptions.description: Translation copies DNA into RNA, and transcription makes protein.

title: The genetic code
definition: The genetic code maps mRNA to protein in three-nucleotide codons: 64 triplet codons specify 20 amino acids and three nonsense (stop) codons, so it is degenerate, with several codons for most amino acids. Translation starts at AUG (methionine), and almost every species uses the same code.
intro: The dictionary from bases to amino acids.

constraints.text: Codons are three nucleotides; 64 codons specify 20 amino acids plus 3 stop codons.
The code is degenerate: most amino acids have more than one codon.
AUG is the start codon (methionine); almost every species uses the same code.

misconceptions.label: one codon, many amino acids
misconceptions.description: One codon can code for several different amino acids.

misconceptions.label: codons are two bases
misconceptions.description: Each codon is two nucleotides long.

title: Transcription
definition: In transcription RNA polymerase, recruited by a promoter sequence, synthesizes mRNA 5'→3' as a copy complementary to the template strand of DNA, with uracil in place of thymine. In eukaryotes transcription factors bind the promoter first, and RNA polymerase II, located in the nucleus, makes the protein-coding pre-mRNAs.
intro: Copying one gene into RNA.

constraints.text: RNA polymerase binds at the promoter and synthesizes RNA 5'→3' from the template strand.
The mRNA is complementary to the template strand, with uracil pairing with adenine instead of thymine.
In eukaryotes transcription factors bind the promoter, and RNA polymerase II in the nucleus makes pre-mRNA.

misconceptions.label: transcription needs a primer
misconceptions.description: RNA polymerase needs a primer to start, like DNA polymerase.

misconceptions.label: the RNA copy contains T
misconceptions.description: The mRNA copy of the template contains thymine.

title: RNA processing in eukaryotes
definition: In the nucleus a eukaryotic pre-mRNA gets a 5' methylguanosine cap and a 3' poly-A tail, which protect it and help export it, and is spliced: introns are removed and exons joined. Only finished mRNA leaves the nucleus.
intro: The finishing steps before an mRNA may leave the nucleus.

constraints.text: A 5' cap and a 3' poly-A tail protect the mRNA from degradation and help its export.
Splicing removes introns (noncoding) and joins exons (expressed).
This processing happens in the nucleus of eukaryotes; prokaryotic mRNA is not capped or spliced.

misconceptions.label: exons are removed
misconceptions.description: Splicing cuts out the exons and keeps the introns.

misconceptions.label: bacteria splice too
misconceptions.description: Bacterial mRNAs are capped and spliced like eukaryotic ones.

title: Translation
definition: At the ribosome the mRNA is read codon by codon from the AUG start. Each charged tRNA's anticodon pairs with a codon in the A site; its amino acid is joined by a peptide bond to the chain held in the P site, and the ribosome moves on three nucleotides. A stop codon brings a release factor that frees the protein.
intro: Reading the message and building the chain.

constraints.text: Translation starts at AUG (methionine) and reads codons three nucleotides at a time.
tRNAs carry amino acids; a tRNA's anticodon base-pairs with the mRNA codon.
Charged tRNAs enter the A site and peptide bonds join each amino acid to the chain at the P site; a stop codon brings a release factor.

misconceptions.label: a tRNA reads stop
misconceptions.description: A tRNA carrying a 'stop' amino acid binds the stop codon.

misconceptions.label: ribosomes read DNA
misconceptions.description: The ribosome reads the DNA directly to build the protein.

# State of Play at the Frontier **This course builds on our AGI Strategy Course and is the successor course Units 4–8 of our earlier 12-week AI Governance course. You can still access the old curriculum [here](https://bluedot.org/courses/governance/1/1).** By the end of it you should be able to show up more credibly in governance conversations. That means being able to consume lots of (technical) information critically, assess what it actually tells you, and translate it for people who need to make decisions. This unit - and this course - work toward building this skill. For Unit 1 you will read the two of the main sources of capability information available (from labs in the form of model cards and from other orgs in the form of independent evaluations), understand what they can and can't tell you, and turn that into a practice brief. But first, let us establish a shared definition of what we mean by Frontier AI Governance. For this course, it's the practice of shaping how advanced AI is built and deployed to achieve good outcomes - it does this primarily through policy, institutions, norms, and relationships. It requires both analytical judgment (what would actually work?) and political judgment (what's achievable, and how do

I help make it happen?) and is as much a research effort as it is an implementation effort. Currently this course operates more so at a strategic/theoretical lens - we are planning to build a more policy focused version soon too. Why strategy first? The AI governance field is characterized by a fair amount of disagreement over goals and methods. This makes it even more important to be able to thoroughly evaluate proposals and build the influence to move the ones one believes in. **Evaluating Claims** Throughout this unit - and, hopefully your future career - you'll encounter many claims about AI capabilities and risks. Here is a quick template to give you an initial method for processing them. Apply it to the readings below and see if you find it useful. - Claim - What is being asserted? By whom? In what context? - Evidence - What evaluations, baselines, or comparisons support it? How robust is the methodology? - External validity - What does this not tell us about real-world interaction/ability? What gap exists between the test and the deployment context? Where are we looking to get to? - Threshold relevance - Would this change a policy stance, trigger an oversight action, or cross

a safety framework threshold? Does it lock us into a certain path? - Missing info - What would you ask for in a hearing, RFI, or expert consultation? title: Model safety evaluations
definition: Model safety evaluations assess model outputs and capabilities; an output test alone does not establish what a user can accomplish in the world.
intro: Read the source excerpt, then explain the mechanism in your own words. Scenarios are original practice exercises.

constraints.text: They evaluate outputs or the ability to perform tasks.
Capability evidence alone does not establish real-world user impact.

misconceptions.label: Overstated inference
misconceptions.description: A model's correct technical answer proves that a user can successfully carry out the corresponding real-world task.

parts.text: In general, evaluations fall into two categories: those that evaluate the outputs of models alone (referred to here as model safety evaluations) and those that evaluate how models impact real-world outcomes like user behavior, decision-making, or other connected systems (referred to here as contextual safety evaluations). Differentiating between these categories is important: understanding whether a model is capable of providing specific information is different from knowing whether a model’s information is helpful to a malicious actor. The questions that guide a model safety evaluation are largely related to the ability to generate specific outputs (“is the model capable?”). Questions may include: Can the model perform a specific task, whether desirable or undesirable? How accurate and reliable are the model’s outputs? How good is a model at answering general-purpose questions? Specific questions? What outputs can the model not provide? Are there areas in which the model is unlikely to provide correct answers? What systemic flaws, biases, or limitations are present in model outputs? How do capabilities compare between models, or over time?
Study focus: Model safety evaluations assess model outputs and capabilities; an output test alone does not establish what a user can accomplish in the world.

title: Contextual safety evaluations
definition: Contextual safety evaluations assess effects on users or connected systems rather than only the quality of model outputs.
intro: Read the source excerpt, then explain the mechanism in your own words. Scenarios are original practice exercises.

constraints.text: They measure user behavior or system-wide outcomes.
Comparing task outcomes with and without model access can test whether access helps users.

misconceptions.label: Overstated inference
misconceptions.description: Judging the factual accuracy of isolated model responses is sufficient to measure effects on users.

parts.text: Contextual safety evaluations measure aspects of human behavior or system-wide impacts. For example, they may monitor how often users successfully complete a given task with or without access to an AI model, or ask them to rate the model’s usefulness. It is important to keep in mind that many of the metrics one could choose for an AI safety evaluation are proxies for the actual risk under consideration, and are therefore imperfect measures of risk. This means that safety evaluations for biological risks thankfully do not actually involve executing biological attacks, but it also unfortunately means that safety evaluations can only measure intermediary factors, like whether an AI model could provide relevant information or reduce the amount of planning time in a controlled, hypothetical scenario. Nevertheless, these evaluations offer an important window into the state of AI safety. Understanding their limitations is key to using them effectively. 2. How to measure it Once a decision about what to measure has been made, the next step is to determine how to measure it. A variety of approaches for AI safety evaluations already exist for both model and contextual safety evaluations.
Study focus: Contextual safety evaluations assess effects on users or connected systems rather than only the quality of model outputs.

title: Evaluation proxies
definition: An evaluation proxy measures an intermediary factor rather than the real-world risk itself, so interpreting it requires attention to what it omits.
intro: Read the source excerpt, then explain the mechanism in your own words. Scenarios are original practice exercises.

constraints.text: Evaluation metrics can be imperfect intermediaries for actual risk.
A result must be interpreted within the limits of the measured outcome.

misconceptions.label: Overstated inference
misconceptions.description: An evaluation proxy measures actual real-world risk without an inferential gap.

parts.text: It is important to keep in mind that many of the metrics one could choose for an AI safety evaluation are proxies for the actual risk under consideration, and are therefore imperfect measures of risk. This means that safety evaluations for biological risks thankfully do not actually involve executing biological attacks, but it also unfortunately means that safety evaluations can only measure intermediary factors, like whether an AI model could provide relevant information or reduce the amount of planning time in a controlled, hypothetical scenario. Nevertheless, these evaluations offer an important window into the state of AI safety. Understanding their limitations is key to using them effectively. 2. How to measure it Once a decision about what to measure has been made, the next step is to determine how to measure it. A variety of approaches for AI safety evaluations already exist for both model and contextual safety evaluations. For example, existing model safety evaluations interrogate an AI system’s ability to complete a particular task or provide certain types of information. One approach is to employ capability testing methods, which typically measure a model’s ability to perform a given task, to specifically probe for capabilities that are considered “risky” or undesirable.

title: Capability jaggedness
definition: Capability jaggedness means that expert performance in one domain can coexist with failures on simpler tasks elsewhere, limiting inference from one benchmark to overall competence.
intro: Read the source excerpt, then explain the mechanism in your own words. Scenarios are original practice exercises.

constraints.text: Capability can vary substantially across domains and tasks.

parts.text: The importance of getting the regulatory response to a truly transformative technology right is obvious. The complexity of the problem may not be. parts.text: A theory of victory for AI governance combines an endgame with a plausible and prescriptive strategy to achieve it. It should also be robust across a range of future scenarios, given uncertainty about key strategic parameters. Nuclear risk provides a relevant case study. Shortly after the development of nuclear weapons, scientists, policymakers, and public figures proposed various theories of victory for nuclear risk, some of which are striking in their similarity to theories of victory for AI risk. Those considered included an international nuclear development moratorium, as well as unilateral enforcement of a monopoly on nuclear weapons. We discuss three potential theories of victory for AI governance. The first is an AI moratorium, in which international coordination indefinitely prevents AI development beyond a certain threshold. This would require an unprecedented level of global coordination and tight control over access to compute. Key challenges include the strong incentives to develop AI for strategic advantage, and the historical difficulty of achieving this level of global coordination. The second theory of victory is an "AI Leviathan" — a single well-controlled AI system or AI-enhanced agency that is empowered to enforce existential security.

parts.text: At its core, radical optionality is about preserving democratic governments’ ability to make good decisions about how to govern transformative AI systems as circumstances evolve. In the short term, this means avoiding overregulation while rapidly building the institutions, information channels and legal authorities needed to respond competently to a broad range of scenarios. The argument for focusing on optionality is simple, and—if you accept a few reasonable assumptions—compelling. These assumptions are: That there is a real possibility of transformative AI (defined as “AI that precipitates a transition comparable to (or more significant than) the agricultural or industrial revolution”) being developed within the next ten years; That profound uncertainty exists as to what capabilities transformative AI systems will possess, what benefits and risks they will generate, and what the best ways for society to capture the benefits while mitigating the risks will be; That a transformatively impactful dual-use technology with significant national security implications will inevitably require some degree of government oversight; and That building the institutional capacity required to effectively govern transformative AI systems will take years, and that society therefore cannot afford to wait until transformative capabilities have actually been developed. Justifying the first assumption is beyond the scope of this paper.

parts.text: Our approach involves analyzing common assumptions across various proposals (as these assumptions are foundational elements for the success of multiple proposals), as well as unique assumptions across individual proposals, by answering three questions: What risks are important to mitigate and who should have primary oversight of frontier AI? Who is delegated tasks and able to play a role? Would the proposed mechanisms or tools actually achieve the proposal’s objectives? We apply this analytic approach to five U.S.-centric AI governance proposals that originate from industry, academia, civil society, and the federal and state governments. These proposals are generally aimed at governing frontier AI systems, which possess cutting-edge capabilities and therefore pose some of the most challenging questions for AI governance. Our analysis reveals that most proposals view AI-enabling talent and AI processes and frameworks as important enablers of AI governance. However, proposals lack consensus regarding the techniques that are most effective at mitigating AI risks and harms. # Grappling with the Intelligence Explosion Now the stress test: what happens to the strategies you compared in Unit 3 if AI itself substantially accelerates research and technological change? Forethought sets out the scenario. CSET gives you competing models of what research automation could look like; OpenAI's account of its own internal workflows is the closest thing we have to evidence. More code, more experiments, and more agents doesn't automatically mean proportionately faster progress - look for where humans and compute still bottleneck, how the tasks were chosen, and whether capability research and safety research would accelerate equally. Most of what you've read assumes the problem is control: who does what with AI. Nielsen asks whether that's even the right frame. Superintelligence Strategy asks what survives if states race regardless. Ngo's efficiency-vs-robustness frame asks what the reflex to centralize would cost. ## Reading resources ### Preparing for the Intelligence Explosion https://www.forethought.org/research/preparing-for-the-intelligence-explosion Read the introduction, Section 5, and one grand challenge of your choice from Section 4. ### When AI Builds AI https://cset.georgetown.edu/wp-content/uploads/CSET-When-AI-Builds-AI.pdf Read the executive summary and "How Far Could AI R&D Automation Go?" (pp. 10–15). ### Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/ Read the first three sections and the methods appendix. ### Superintelligence

Strategy https://www.nationalsecurity.ai/ In Unit 3 you took a pass at different governance proposals and stress-tested them against each other. This reading stress-tests them against something else - the geopolitical reality that states will race, and no proposal survives if it assumes they won't. This is maybe the most concrete attempt to work within race dynamics rather than wishing them away. Introducing Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (MAIM): if you can't stop the race, can you create deterrence that stabilizes it? Any state's aggressive bid for unilateral AI dominance gets met with preventive sabotage by rivals - from cyberattacks to kinetic strikes on datacenters. This in my opinion already roughly describes the strategic picture, at least from a more realist lens. But red lines are unclear, observability is a nightmare, and sabotage delays but doesn't deny progress. The "wicked problems" chart distinguishes tame technical subproblems from genuinely unsolved governance challenges. It's also a direct challenge to the Manhattan Project framing (a la Aschenbrenner) - arguing that a unilateral bid invites sabotage rather than securing advantage. ### AI-Enabled Coups: How a Small Group Could Use AI to Seize Power https://www.forethought.org/research/ai-enabled-coups-how-a-small-group-could-use-ai-to-seize-power If you have not yet read this, read it! ### Extreme Power Concentration https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/extreme-power-concentration/ Good starting point for

thinking about this more - features gradual disempowerment as well. ### ASI existential risk: reconsidering alignment as a goal https://michaelnotebook.com/xriskbrief/ Most readings here operate within a broader but still contained AI governance paradigm - they assume the task at hand is controlling who does what with AI (including AI's doing stuff themselves, but they already struggled there), and debate how. This reading asks whether that's even the right frame. Nielsen argues the fundamental danger isn't rogue AI getting out of control. It's the raw power that deep understanding of reality confers on whoever has it. "Recipes for ruin" become accessible. Regulatory frameworks manage deployment but can't contain knowledge once it exists. He names d/acc and coceleration as alternative strategies but also says: "I don't see a full through line to this working." If Nielsen is right that the fundamental problem is power conferred rather than control lost, what does that mean for every proposal you've evaluated since Unit 3? ### Distributed vs centralized agents https://www.mindthefuture.info/p/distributed-vs-centralized-agents The centralization/decentralization tension has been running through the course since the start. This I think is not a matter of policy preferences but rather a structural thing. Ngo's post is about agents in the abstract: centralized ones are more efficient,

distributed ones more robust, and he wants both. The governance reading is mine, not his. After three readings about acceleration, coups, and deterrence, you may want to quite naturally centralize - build oversight, give institutions teeth, monitor everything. Unfortunately, that's also how you get lock-in, capture, and abuse. There is no clean exit from this - where did you land on the centralization spectrum in Unit 3? parts.text: Advanced AI removes this constraint, making it technologically feasible to replace human workers with AI systems that are singularly loyal to just one person. # How should we handle open weights as models get more capable? The relevant question used to be "should we be open?" - kind of like asking whether we should connect our very best AI models to the internet. We all know how that went. But that question is no longer live. Open models are now genuinely good, and there are a lot of them. Beyond the models themselves, we're seeing open training code, data, RL environments, and checkpoints. Training 70B+ models on decentralized consumer hardware is feasible. With a single H100, you can run plenty of models downloaded from HuggingFace - where you'll also find lovely abliterated and unsafe variants. That said, open models do provide real economic benefits, enable privacy-conscious adoption, and draw power away from the closed frontier labs. ## Reading resources ### Open-Sourcing Highly Capable Foundation Models: An evaluation of risks, benefits, and alternative methods for pursuing open-source objectives https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.09227 Read the section on alternative ways to pursue open-source objectives. ### On the Societal Impact of Open Foundation Models https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07918 Kapoor et al.'s 2024 marginal-risk framework for open foundation models. ### Beyond DeepSeek: China's Diverse Open-Weight AI Ecosystem and Its Policy Implications https://hai.stanford.edu/policy/beyond-deepseek-chinas-diverse-open-weight-ai-ecosystem-and-its-policy-implications Stanford HAI on China's open-weight ecosystem and what

its global adoption means for US policy. ### Open models in perpetual catch-up https://www.interconnects.ai/p/open-models-in-perpetual-catch-up Lambert on open models sitting a steady 6–9 months behind the closed frontier, with Chinese labs dominating. ### Distributed and Decentralized Training: Technical Governance Challenges in a Shifting AI Landscape https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07765 Read the abstract and the governance-challenges section: how distributed and decentralized training erode compute governance. ### When is it important that open-weight models aren't released? https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/TeF8Az2EiWenR9APF/when-is-it-important-that-open-weight-models-aren-t-released Greenblatt's 2025 conditional argument for when open-weight release becomes too dangerous. ### International AI Safety Report 2026 - Extended Summary for Policymakers https://internationalaisafetyreport.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/ai-safety-report-2026-extended-summary-for-policymakers.pdf Read Section 3.4, "Open-weight models". ## Exercises ### Write ~1 page on where you stand! 1. title: If-then commitments
definition: An if-then commitment links a specified capability condition to required risk mitigations, potentially delaying deployment or development until those mitigations are ready.
intro: Read the source excerpt, then explain the mechanism in your own words. Scenarios are original practice exercises.

parts.text: This piece is a primer on an emerging framework for handling this challenge: if-then commitments. These are commitments of the form: If an AI model has capability X, risk mitigations Y must be in place. And, if needed, we will delay AI deployment and/or development to ensure the mitigations can be present in time. A specific example: If an AI model has the ability to walk a novice through constructing a weapon of mass destruction, we must ensure that there are no easy ways for consumers to elicit behavior in this category from the AI model. If-then commitments can be voluntarily adopted by AI developers; they also, potentially, can be enforced by regulators. Adoption of if-then commitments could help reduce risks from AI in two key ways: (a) prototyping, battle-testing, and building consensus around a potential framework for regulation; and (b) helping AI developers and others build roadmaps of what risk mitigations need to be in place by when. Such adoption does not require agreement on whether major AI risks are imminent—a polarized topic—only that certain situations would require certain risk mitigations if they came to pass. Three industry leaders—Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic—have published relatively detailed frameworks along these lines.
Study focus: An if-then commitment links a specified capability condition to required risk mitigations, potentially delaying deployment or development until those mitigations are ready.

# When, if ever, should frontier development be slowed - and by whom? When should frontier development be slowed, what exactly should be restricted, and who decides? Revisit your Unit 3 position now that you've been through Unit 4's acceleration analysis. The four short readings at the top are four different kinds of thing: a public ask (Pacing the Frontier), a company's conditional promise (the RSP), a report of what one lab actually did (OpenAI on pacing), and a draft treaty (MIRI). Then Carlsmith against the RSP and the treaty: individual vs. collective restraint, and what he calls "greenlighting" - who gets to say a lab may proceed. Ask where the work and the compute go when something is restricted. Finally, test your preferred mechanism against Bostrom and Belrose: does it delay benefits that matter, obstruct safety work, create an overhang, or concentrate power? And what would you actually do with the time it buys? ## Reading resources ### Pacing the Frontier https://www.pacingthefrontier.com/ Statement by 1,386 frontier-lab employees asking the US government to back an international effort to build tools for pacing frontier development. ### When AI builds itself https://www.anthropic.com/institute/recursive-self-improvement Read "What should we do?". ### An Alien Mind https://openai.com/index/an-alien-mind/ Read "Pacing RSI" and the

parts.text: In a nutshell: The US federal government is likely to be the most consequential regulator of AI in the world, with jurisdiction over the most prominent AI companies and the chip supply chain. Working in government could position you to support better policy ideas and — perhaps more importantly — help to ensure that those ideas are implemented effectively. At the same time, the path to influence is long and politically constrained, the culture isn’t for everyone, and the potential for impact comes with a risk of making things worse. Pros: Windows of opportunity in policy can open and close quickly, and being inside government positions you to act when they do. Implementation is often a bigger bottleneck than good ideas — government roles let you work on the part that actually matters. Cons: These roles often have long hours, low job security, and high turnover. Many roles are partisan, meaning your options are constrained by which party holds power. Higher risk of inadvertently doing harm than most other governance paths. Key facts on fit: Most federal roles require US citizenship and willingness to live in or regularly travel to DC.

Becoming one of those people is partly about knowing your stuff and partly about being someone others like and trust. It’s also worth being honest with yourself about whether you’d thrive in the political environment. Washington has a particular culture: it’s heavy on networking, status, and influence. Merit — having the right ideas or delivering results — isn’t the only driver of success. People who find that culture draining or off-putting should think carefully about whether this is the right path, or whether a different role in AI policy (such as research or technical governance) might be a better fit. # Finding Your Leverage Point You've spent five units reading the field, mapping it, evaluating its proposals, and taking at least an initial position on one of its most contested questions. Now our final question is more personal: given everything you know - what do you do? For this Unit the focus will be less on "what should the world do" but rather on "what should you do, given who you are and what you know now." So let's write it out! Write some amount of pages (bullets are fine) covering: **What do you now believe? (~20 min)** - Your worldview - revisit the positions you covered during the course, but try to zoom out. What's your overall picture of where AI (governance) is heading? Be honest about your confidence levels and unknowns (also known as learning opportunities). - Try to be specific about your remaining uncertainties. For this find and name the 2-3 uncertainties that, if resolved, would change what you think should be done significantly. Some prompts if you get stuck: - How urgent is all of this? Are we in a "years to get it right" or "months to get it right" situation? How many shots on goal do we get? -

What's the failure mode you're most worried about? - Which of the Strategic Visions from Unit 3 do you now find most plausible - and has that changed since you first read them? - What's the most important thing you learned in this course that you didn't know before? - What do you now believe that you didn't believe a few weeks ago? What do you believe less strongly? **What needs to be done? (~15 min)** Try to identify 3-5 specific things that you think need to/should happen/should be looked into. Ideally these are concrete and actionable. For each, ask: - Is anyone doing this well right now? If yes, do they need help? If no, why not - is it a gap or is it intractable? Where is it on the spectrum? - What's the main bottleneck? Is it talent, funding, lack of solution, political will, lack of a forcing event, technical knowledge, institutional capacity, or something else? - How does this connect to your positions on these things? **What should you do? (~25 min)** Be honest with yourself. List your assets/gaps. What do you bring? Consider: - Domain expertise (law, policy, finance, biology, security, engineering, etc.) - Technical skills (coding, data analysis, research

methods, model evaluation) - Communication and writing ability. Can you explain technical things to non-specialists? Can you write clearly under time pressure? Do you enjoy it? - Existing platform or audience. Do people already listen to you? A newsletter, a professional community, a social media following, a reputation in a niche. If you have zero, building one is probably a good step one. - Professional network and access. Who can you reach that others can't? - Institutional position. Where are you, and what does that let you do? Inside a lab, inside government, inside a university, inside an industry being transformed by AI? - Geographic location. DC? London? SF? Brussels? Beijing? Nairobi? Somewhere else? - Unusual combinations of all the above and below. - Operational and organizational ability. Can you manage projects, hire people, run events, raise money, build organizations? - Stage of career and positioning. - Can you go full-time on this? Or do you have 5 hours a week? - Can you take a financial risk? Do you need stability? Can you self-fund a project for 6 months, or do you need a salary from day one? - Your comparative advantage - what's the most impactful work where you already have an edge?

**Forcing questions to make you stop hedging.** - Gun to your head: you can only work on one thing for the next 6 months. What is it? One thing. Write it down. - You receive a $1M grant tomorrow. How do you spend it? You can fund yourself, fund others, start something, or support something that exists. Be specific! **A few more:** - It's 2030 and things have gone badly. An AI-related catastrophe has occurred (maybe we’re all dead). Looking back (just before you die), what do you wish you had started working on today? - It's 2030 and things have gone well. Things are working better than expected. What happened, and what role did you play? - Who are three people you should be talking to that you're not currently talking to? **Given your answers above, set out what your next move is going to be:** - A specific action you're going to take in the next 30 days. (Apply for X, reach out to Y, start learning Z, write a piece on W, start a Substack about V.) - A 6-month plan for building toward a position where you can contribute. the path?) Then bring in the red team (aka your discussion group, your friends, Claude). Ask them: What's the strongest argument that your plan is wrong?
